"'''Money for Nothing'''" is a song by the British [[Rock music|rock]] band [[Dire Straits]], the second track on their fifth studio album ''[[Brothers in Arms (album)|Brothers in Arms]]'' (1985). It was released as the album's second single on 28 June 1985 through [[Vertigo Records]]. The song's lyrics are written from the point of view of two working-class men watching music videos and commenting on what they see. The song features a guest appearance by [[Sting (musician)|Sting]], who sings the signature [[falsetto]] introduction, background vocals and a backing chorus of "[[MTV#"I Want My MTV!"|I want my MTV]]" set to the same notes as the verses of [[the Police]]'s hit "[[Don't Stand So Close to Me|Don't Stand So Close To Me]]".<ref>{{cite web|first= Martin |last= Kielty |title= When Mark Knopfler and Sting Connected for 'Money for Nothing' |website= [[Ultimate Classic Rock]] |date= 24 June 2019 |access-date= 7 December 2020 |url= https://ultimateclassicrock.com/mark-knopfler-sting-money-for-nothing/}}</ref> The groundbreaking [[Steve Barron]]-directed music video, one of the first uses of computer-animated human characters, was the first to be aired on [[MTV Europe]] when the network launched on 1 August 1987.<ref>{{cite news|title= MTV ready to rock Russia |work= [[BBC News Online]] |date= 25 September 1998 |access-date= 1 April 2007 |url= https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/178641.stm |quote= But the channel's continental incarnation - MTV Europe - ... was launched in 1987 with the first video - beamed into 1.6 million paying households - being Dire Straits' Money for Nothing.}}</ref>

"Money for Nothing" peaked at number one for three weeks on both the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and [[Rock Top Tracks]] chart and at number four in the band's native UK. In July 1985, the month following its release, Dire Straits and Sting performed the song at [[Live Aid]]. At the [[28th Annual Grammy Awards]] in 1986, "Money for Nothing" won [[Grammy Award for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal|Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal]] and was nominated for [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]] and [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year|Song of the Year]] as well. At the [[1986 MTV Video Music Awards]], the music video received 11 nominations, winning [[MTV Video Music Award for Video of the Year|Video of the Year]] and [[MTV Video Music Award for Best Group Video|Best Group Video]]. It is considered one of the band's signature songs.

Until 2026, the sound of Sting’s "MTV" in the introduction just prior to the drum [[cadenza]]<!-- that one consists of notes D-G-A; there are three more prior in the full version which are D-G-G --> served as the audio for [[MTV Entertainment Studios]] production credit title card.

"Money for Nothing" is a song by the British rock band Dire Straits, the second track on their fifth studio album Brothers in Arms (1985). It was released as the album's second single on 28 June 1985 through Vertigo Records. The song's lyrics are written from the point of view of two working-class men watching music videos and commenting on what they see. The song features a guest appearance by Sting, who sings the signature falsetto introduction, background vocals and a backing chorus of "I want my MTV" set to the same notes as the verses of the Police's hit "Don't Stand So Close To Me". The groundbreaking Steve Barron-directed music video, one of the first uses of computer-animated human characters, was the first to be aired on MTV Europe when the network launched on 1 August 1987.

"Money for Nothing" peaked at number one for three weeks on both the US Billboard Hot 100 and Rock Top Tracks chart and at number four in the band's native UK. In July 1985, the month following its release, Dire Straits and Sting performed the song at Live Aid. At the 28th Annual Grammy Awards in 1986, "Money for Nothing" won Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal and was nominated for Record of the Year and Song of the Year as well. At the 1986 MTV Video Music Awards, the music video received 11 nominations, winning Video of the Year and Best Group Video. It is considered one of the band's signature songs.

Until 2026, the sound of Sting’s "MTV" in the introduction just prior to the drum cadenza served as the audio for MTV Entertainment Studios production credit title card.

sections.heading: Composition
Music
sections.wikitext:
"Money for Nothing" is a [[pop rock]] song.<ref>{{cite web|first= James |last= Rose |title= 30 Years Since: Dire Straits' 'Brothers in Arms' Album |website= [[Daily Review (website)|Daily Review]] |date= 15 September 2015 |access-date= 28 October 2019 |url= https://dailyreview.com.au/30-years-since-dire-straits-brothers-in-arms-album/ |quote= The opening tracks are pretty conventional pop-rock chart shooters}}</ref> As per keyboardist [[Alan Clark (keyboardist)|Alan Clark]], the song started as a more [[The Rolling Stones|Rolling Stones]]-like track in rehearsals, before Knopfler came up with the song's riff while improvising in the studio.<ref>{{cite magazine|first=James|last=McNair|title=Dire straits go supernova with Brothers in Arms|date=18 February 2020|magazine=Mojo|url=https://gb.readly.com/magazines/mojo/2020-02-18/5e444f5316ddae658ce98788?srsltid=AfmBOopThVo35XxYZca2gEsmOxpSs-6R8J7N99I1CZK_kabdEbReAJ-i}}{{subscription required}}</ref> They had also stumbled on the guitar sound by accident, so Knopfler recorded his guitar parts to a click track to get the song down, then the rest of the track was constructed via [[overdubbing]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Episode 465: Dire Straits' Alan Clark |url=https://podcasts.apple.com/gb/podcast/episode-465-dire-straits-alan-clark/id303040265?i=1000531750710 |access-date=2026-08-22 |website=Apple Podcasts |language=en-GB}}</ref> Knopfler modeled his guitar sound on [[ZZ Top]] guitarist [[Billy Gibbons]]'s trademark guitar tone, as ZZ Top's music videos were already a staple of early MTV. Gibbons told [[Timothy White (writer)|Timothy White]] of ''[[Musician (magazine)|Musician]]'' in late 1985 that Knopfler had solicited his help in replicating the tone, adding, "He didn't do a half-bad job, either, considering that I never told him a goddamned thing!"<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Timothy |last= White |authorlink= Timothy White (writer) |title= ZZ Top: The Ongoing Legend of Texan Rock's Rough Boys |magazine= [[Musician (magazine)|Musician]] |publisher= Amordian Press |date= January 1986 |issue= 87 |page= 65 |quote= 'I gotta hand it to that Mark Knopfler for the "Money For Nothing" number on that last Dire Straits album. That guy must have called me three or four times to find out what I did with my guitar so that he could copy it for that song.' He pushes the brim back on his golf cap and smiles, the flawless pearly whites gleaming. 'He didn't do a half-bad job, either, considering that I never told him a goddamned thing!'}}</ref>

Following the initial sessions in [[Montserrat]] where they recorded the main guitar part, Neil Dorfsman tried to recreate the sound in subsequent sessions at the Power Station in New York but was unsuccessful.<ref name=":0">{{cite magazine|first= Richard |last= Buskin |title= Classic Tracks: Dire Straits 'Money For Nothing' |magazine= [[Sound on Sound]] |date= May 2006 |access-date= 23 July 2014 |url= http://www.soundonsound.com/sos/may06/articles/classictracks_0506.htm}}</ref> At one stage, drummer [[Terry Williams (drummer)|Terry Williams]]' parts became an issue, so they ended up recruiting session musician [[Omar Hakim]] to re-do them; Williams' intro and tom-tom fills throughout the song were kept, while Hakim played the straight beat.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Jackson |first=Blair |date=1999-02-01 |title=Classic Tracks: Dire Straits' "Money for Nothing" |url=https://www.mixonline.com/recording/classic-tracks/classic-tracks-dire-straits-money-nothing-372507 |access-date=2026-08-22 |website=Mixonline |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Schlosberg |first=Karen |date=May 1986 |title=Terry Williams — Strait Foundation |url=https://www.moderndrummer.com/article/may-1986-terry-williams-strait-foundation/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200918200617/https:/www.moderndrummer.com/article/may-1986-terry-williams-strait-foundation/ |archive-date=2020-09-18 |access-date=2026-08-22 |work=Modern Drummer |language=en-US}}</ref>
sections.text:
"Money for Nothing" is a pop rock song. As per keyboardist Alan Clark, the song started as a more Rolling Stones-like track in rehearsals, before Knopfler came up with the song's riff while improvising in the studio. They had also stumbled on the guitar sound by accident, so Knopfler recorded his guitar parts to a click track to get the song down, then the rest of the track was constructed via overdubbing. Knopfler modeled his guitar sound on ZZ Top guitarist Billy Gibbons's trademark guitar tone, as ZZ Top's music videos were already a staple of early MTV. Gibbons told Timothy White of Musician in late 1985 that Knopfler had solicited his help in replicating the tone, adding, "He didn't do a half-bad job, either, considering that I never told him a goddamned thing!"

Following the initial sessions in Montserrat where they recorded the main guitar part, Neil Dorfsman tried to recreate the sound in subsequent sessions at the Power Station in New York but was unsuccessful. At one stage, drummer Terry Williams' parts became an issue, so they ended up recruiting session musician Omar Hakim to re-do them; Williams' intro and tom-tom fills throughout the song were kept, while Hakim played the straight beat.

sections.heading: Lyrics
sections.wikitext:
[[Mark Knopfler]] described the writing of the song in a 1985 interview with author [[Bill Flanagan]]:

{{quote|The lead character in "Money for Nothing" is a guy who works in the hardware department in a television/{{zwsp}}custom kitchen/{{zwsp}}refrigerator/{{zwsp}}microwave appliance store. He's singing the song. I wrote the song when I was actually in the store. I borrowed a bit of paper and started to write the song down in the store. I wanted to use a lot of the language that the real guy actually used when I heard him, because it was more real....<ref name="CBSC2">{{cite web|title= Review of the Atlantic Regional Panel decision in CHOZ-FM re the song "Money for Nothing" by Dire Straits |publisher= [[Canadian Broadcast Standards Council]] |date= 17 May 2011 |url= http://www.cbsc.ca/english/decisions/2011/110831.php |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140810054301/http://www.cbsc.ca/english/decisions/2011/110831.php |archive-date= 10 August 2014|access-date=10 May 2023}}</ref>}}

In 2000, Knopfler appeared on ''[[Parkinson (TV series)|Parkinson]]'' on [[BBC One]] and further explained where the lyrics originated. According to Knopfler, he had visited an appliance store in New York City. At the back of the store, a wall of televisions were all tuned to MTV. Knopfler said that standing next to him, watching the TVs, there was a male employee, dressed in a baseball cap, work boots, and a checkered shirt, who was delivering boxes. As they watched MTV, the man said things like, "What are those, Hawaiian noises?... That ain't workin'," etc. Knopfler requested a pen to write some of these lines down, and eventually put them to music.<ref name="CBSC2"/>
The [[First-person narrative|first-person narrator]] in the lyrics describes a musician "banging on the bongos like a chimpanzee" and a woman "stickin' in the camera - Man, we could have some fun". In the second verse, the performer is described as "that little [[Faggot (slang)|faggot]] with the earring and the make-up", and the narrator bemoans that these artists get "Money for nothing and chicks for free."<ref>{{cite web|first= Matthew |last= Lasar |title= Canada wants unedited "Money for Nothing" back on the radio |website= [[Ars Technica]] |date= 24 January 2011 |access-date= 27 November 2012 |url= https://arstechnica.com/business/2011/01/canadas-much-ado-about-money-for-nothing/}}</ref>

The songwriting credits are shared between Mark Knopfler and [[Sting (musician)|Sting]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Dire Straits: Money for Nothing |website= AllMusic |url= http://www.allmusic.com/song/money-for-nothing-mt0011279271/lyrics |archive-date= 23 June 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150623063049/http://www.allmusic.com/song/money-for-nothing-mt0011279271/lyrics}}</ref> According to Knopfler, he used the network slogan "I want my MTV" after seeing an [[MTV]] advertisement featuring [[The Police (band)|The Police]] and setting it to the tune of "[[Don't Stand So Close to Me]]" (written by Sting), hence the cowriting credit.<ref>[https://ultimateclassicrock.com/mark-knopfler-sting-money-for-nothing/ When Mark Knopfler and Sting Connected for Money for Nothing] (Ultimate Classic Rock website)</ref> "Sting used to come to Montserrat to go windsurfing," recalled [[John Illsley]], "and he came up for supper at the studio. We played him 'Money for Nothing' and he turned round and said, 'You've done it this time, you bastards.' Mark said if he thought it was so good, why didn't he go and add something to it. He did his bit there and then."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Paul |last= Rees |title= The sultan of swing |magazine= [[Classic Rock (magazine)|Classic Rock]] |issue= 210 |date= June 2015 |page= 124}}</ref>

Sting elaborated on his co-writing credit in a 1987 interview:

{{quote|Mark [Knopfler] asked me to go in the studio and sing this line, "I want my MTV." He gave me the melody, and I thought, "Oh, great, '[[Don't Stand So Close to Me]]', that's a nice quote, it's fun." So I did it, and thought nothing of it, until my publishers, [[Virgin Group|Virgin]] - who I've been at war with for years and who I have no respect for - decided that was a song they owned, 'Don't Stand So Close to Me'. They said that they wanted a percentage of the song, much to my embarrassment. So they took it.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.sting.com/news/title/Interview:%20MUSICIAN%20(1987)|title=Slapping Sting around - Can he handle the tough questions...?|first=Peter|last=Watrous|magazine=Musician|date=December 1987}}</ref>}}

However, keyboardist [[Alan Clark (keyboardist)|Alan Clark]] claims the "I want my MTV" intro was his idea and not Knopfler's. According to him, the song originally began with the guitar riff, and then he developed the intro on keyboards and sang "I want my MTV" on top during a break in rehearsals for the album.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.musicradar.com/news/dire-straits-money-for-nothing-alan-clark-mark-knopfler|first=Daniel|last=Griffiths|website=musicradar.com|title=Dire Straits keyboard player Alan Clark: "When Mark Knopfler first played Money For Nothing, there was no 'I Want My MTV'... the idea was mine"|date=10 March 2022|access-date=28 November 2022}}</ref>

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext:
[[File:Money for Nothing Music Video.jpg|250px|thumb|right|The song's music video features early computer animation.]]
The music video for the song features early 3D [[computer animation]] illustrating the lyrics. The video was one of the first uses of computer-animated human characters and was groundbreaking at the time of its release.<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Claire |last= Schaffer |title= How the Dire Straits' 'Money for Nothing' Video Helped CGI Go Mainstream |magazine= [[Garage Magazine]] |date= 11 March 2019 |access-date= 21 March 2020 |url= https://www.vice.com/en/article/dire-straits-money-for-nothing-video/ |archive-date= 4 April 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190404220734/https://garage.vice.com/en_us/article/9kpmzp/dire-straits-money-for-nothing-video |url-status= live}}</ref>

The video makes references to the following (nonexistent) songs, bands, albums, and labels:
* "Baby, Baby" by [[Első Emelet|First Floor]], from ''Turn Left''; Magyar Records<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://elsoemelet.hu/|website=Elsoemelet.hu|title=Első Emelet együttes|access-date=19 May 2026}}</ref>
* "Sally" by the Ian Pearson Band, from ''Hot Dogs''; Rush Records<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wTP2RUD_cL0&list=RDeJ9uKCBivVY&index=27|title=Dire Straits - Money For Nothing (Official Music Video)|date=23 February 2010|access-date=5 May 2026|via=YouTube}}</ref>  

Originally, Mark Knopfler was not at all enthusiastic about the concept of the music video. MTV, however, was insistent on it. Director [[Steve Barron]], of [[Rushes Postproduction]] in London, was contacted by [[Warner Bros. Records|Warner Bros.]] to persuade Knopfler to relent. Describing the contrasting attitudes of Knopfler and MTV, he said:

{{quote|The problem was that Mark Knopfler was very anti-videos. All he wanted to do was perform, and he thought that videos would destroy the purity of songwriters and performers. They said, "Can you convince him that this is the right thing to do, because we've played this song to MTV and they think it's fantastic but they won't play it if it's him standing there playing guitar. They need a concept."<ref name="rushes">{{cite magazine |first= D. |last= Knight |title= Money For Nothing: The Beginnings of CGI |magazine= Promo Magazine |date= September 2006 |url= http://www.rushes.co.uk/googlef91418d7fca59928.html |access-date= 17 February 2007 |archive-date= 23 November 2022 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20221123000452/http://www.rushes.co.uk/googlef91418d7fca59928.html |url-status= dead }}</ref>}}

Barron then flew to [[Budapest]] to convince Knopfler of their concept. Meeting together after a gig, Knopfler was still unimpressed, but this time his girlfriend was present and took a hand. According to Barron:

{{quote|Luckily, his girlfriend said, "He's absolutely right. There aren't enough interesting videos on MTV, and that sounds like a brilliant idea." Mark didn't say anything but he didn't make the call to get me out of Budapest. We just went ahead and did it.}}

Ian Pearson and Gavin Blair created the animation, using a [[Robert Bosch GmbH|Bosch]] FGS-4000 CGI system<ref name="mvdbase">{{cite web |title= Dire Straits – Money for nothing [version 2] |website= Mvdbase |access-date= 23 July 2014 |url= http://www.mvdbase.com/video.php?id=8683%20mvdbase.com |archive-date= 27 July 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140727012250/http://www.mvdbase.com/video.php?id=8683%20mvdbase.com |url-status= dead }}</ref> and a [[Quantel Paintbox]] system.<ref>{{cite news|first= Liam |last= Allen |title= Adam Ant to Michael Jackson: Shaping the MTV landscape |work= BBC News Online |date= 29 November 2010 |url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-11499628}}</ref> The animators went on to found [[computer animation]] studio Mainframe Entertainment (today [[Mainframe Studios]]), and referenced the "Money for Nothing" video in an episode of their ''[[ReBoot]]'' series called "Talent Night."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Mainframe Studios |title=ReBoot - S01E11 - Talent Night (HD) |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=661pf3EWI9s&t=5m02s |website=YouTube |access-date=7 October 2026}}</ref> The video also includes stage footage of Dire Straits performing, with partially [[Rotoscoping|rotoscoped]] animation in bright neon colours, as seen on the cover of the [[Money for Nothing (album)|compilation album of the same name]].

sections.heading: Notable performances
sections.wikitext: When Dire Straits performed "Money for Nothing" at the 1985 [[Live Aid]] Concert at [[Wembley Stadium (1923)|Wembley Stadium]], the performance featured a guest appearance by Sting. Knopfler performed "Money for Nothing" during the [[Nelson Mandela 70th Birthday Tribute]] and [[the Prince's Trust]] concerts in 1986 with Sting,<ref>{{cite news|first= John J. |last= O'Connor |author-link= John J. O'Connor (journalist) |title= 'All-Star Rock Concert,' on HBO, from London |newspaper= [[The New York Times]] |date= 26 October 1986 |access-date= 15 May 2017 |url= https://www.nytimes.com/1986/10/22/arts/all-star-rock-concert-on-hbo-from-london.html}}</ref> as well as the [[Nordoff-Robbins]] charity show at [[Concerts at Knebworth House|Knebworth]] in 1990. These versions featured extended guitar solos by Knopfler, backed by [[Eric Clapton]] (as guest) and [[Phil Palmer]].
sections.text: When Dire Straits performed "Money for Nothing" at the 1985 Live Aid Concert at Wembley Stadium, the performance featured a guest appearance by Sting. Knopfler performed "Money for Nothing" during the Nelson Mandela 70th Birthday Tribute and the Prince's Trust concerts in 1986 with Sting, as well as the Nordoff-Robbins charity show at Knebworth in 1990. These versions featured extended guitar solos by Knopfler, backed by Eric Clapton (as guest) and Phil Palmer.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]]'' said that it's "a simply rocking cut taking a look at jobs and videos performed by rock stars."<ref name=cb>{{cite magazine|title=Single Releases|magazine=Cash Box|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/80s/1985/CB-1985-07-06.pdf|date=6 July 1985|access-date=3 August 2022|page=9}}</ref> ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' called it a "[[blues]]y poke at [Dire Straits' and Sting's] own kind; intentions ambiguous."<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Billboard|date=6 July 1985|access-date=3 August 2022|page=77|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RCQEAAAAMBAJ|title=Reviews}}</ref>

''[[Rolling Stone]]'' listed the song as the 94th greatest guitar song of all time, noting how Mark Knopfler "traded his pristine, rootsy tone for a dry, over-processed sound achieved by running a [[Gibson Les Paul|Les Paul]] through a [[wah-wah pedal]] on a track that became one of the [MTV] network's earliest hits."<ref>{{cite magazine|title= The 100 Greatest Guitar Songs of All Time |magazine= [[Rolling Stone]] |url= https://www.rollingstone.com/news/coverstory/20947527/page/38 |archive-date= 30 May 2008 |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080530224823/http://www.rollingstone.com/news/coverstory/20947527/page/38}}</ref> ''[[AllMusic]]'' called the song one of Knopfler's finest lyrical moments and the [[Hook (music)|hook]] one of the best and catchiest of the time period.<ref name="AllMusic-Review">{{cite web |last1=Greenwald |first1=Matthew |title=Money for Nothing Review by Matthew Greenwald |url=https://www.allmusic.com/song/money-for-nothing-mt0011279271#review |website=[[AllMusic]] |access-date=18 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120915055545/http://www.allmusic.com/song/money-for-nothing-mt0011279271#review |archive-date=15 September 2012 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2018, ''[[Classic Rock (magazine)|Classic Rock]]'' wrote: "At its core, 'Money For Nothing' was an old-school boogie, but a dash of studio polish, Sting's mannered backing vocal and a computer-generated promo video were enough to turn it, and Dire Straits themselves, into the very embodiment of 80s naff."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.loudersound.com/reviews/album-of-the-week-club-review-dire-straits-brothers-in-arms | title=Album Of The Week Club Review: Dire Straits - Brothers In Arms | work=Louder | date=21 May 2018 | access-date=28 August 2025}}</ref>
sections.text:
Cash Box said that it's "a simply rocking cut taking a look at jobs and videos performed by rock stars." Billboard called it a "bluesy poke at [Dire Straits' and Sting's] own kind; intentions ambiguous."

Rolling Stone listed the song as the 94th greatest guitar song of all time, noting how Mark Knopfler "traded his pristine, rootsy tone for a dry, over-processed sound achieved by running a Les Paul through a wah-wah pedal on a track that became one of the [MTV] network's earliest hits." AllMusic called the song one of Knopfler's finest lyrical moments and the hook one of the best and catchiest of the time period.

In 2018, Classic Rock wrote: "At its core, 'Money For Nothing' was an old-school boogie, but a dash of studio polish, Sting's mannered backing vocal and a computer-generated promo video were enough to turn it, and Dire Straits themselves, into the very embodiment of 80s naff."
